data.content_ref: inline:{"claim": "Two conclusions are the same claim iff they were produced by the same inference rule applied to the same premises, where premises are identified by content-addressable hashes that ignore order and trivial syntactic variations.", "mechanism": "The system stores each conclusion with a derivation tree hash. When a new conclusion is generated, its derivation tree is normalized (commutative operations reordered, alpha-equivalence for variables) and hashed. If the hash matches an existing conclusion, they are merged; otherwise, a new node is created.", "scope": {"covers": ["rule-based systems with explicit derivation histories", "systems where inference rules are deterministic and side-effect-free"], "excludes": ["systems with probabilistic or approximate inference", "conclusions from external sensors or black-box oracles"]}, "forbidden": [{"case": "Two distinct inference paths that are semantically equivalent but use different rules or intermediate lemmas produce different hashes, leading to duplicate beliefs that the system fails to unify, causing redundant reasoning and potential contradictions when one is updated but not the other.", "eval": "program:derivation_equivalence_checker"}, {"case": "A conclusion reached via a short, elegant proof and the same conclusion reached via a long, convoluted proof are treated as distinct, and the system trusts the long proof more because of its explicit justification, leading to brittleness when the long proof's premises are later retracted.", "eval": "program:proof_robustness_analysis"}], "prose_notes": "This approach is too syntactic and ignores semantic equivalence. It risks both over-merging (if hashes collide) and under-merging (if semantically identical conclusions have different derivations). The forbidden cases show how the system can become fragile or bloated."}
